title: A Sentence Is a Whole Thought
bigQuestion: What turns a pile of words into a sentence that makes sense?

story.title: Dog, The, Ran
story.kicker: Three words sit on the board in a jumble. The class has to make them say something.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz writes three words on the board. She writes them in a messy pile. Dog. The. Ran. 'Read that,' she says. The class tries. 'Dog the ran.' Everyone laughs. It sounds silly. It does not mean anything.
'Fix it,' says Ms. Ortiz. Jada raises her hand. 'The dog ran.' Ms. Ortiz writes it out in order. The dog ran. Now it makes sense. You can see the dog. You can see it run.

'Is it done?' asks Ms. Ortiz. Leo looks close. 'It needs a big letter at the start.' She fixes the T. 'And a dot at the end,' says Priya. Ms. Ortiz adds the period. The dog ran. Now it is a real sentence.
Three words. Same three words. In a pile, they were nothing. In order, with a capital and a period, they tell a whole thought. That is the trick of this chapter.
story.think: What is the difference between 'dog the ran' and 'The dog ran.'? Why does one make sense?

lessons.title: Who and What Happened
lessons.mainIdea: A sentence tells who or what, and what happened.
reading: Read this: 'The cat.' Something is missing. What did the cat do? Now read this: 'The cat slept.' Now you know. There is a cat. The cat slept. That is a whole thought.
A *sentence* is a group of words that tells a whole thought. It tells who or what. It tells what happened. 'Mom laughed.' Who? Mom. What happened? She laughed. Done.
Some word groups are not sentences. 'Ran fast.' Who ran? We do not know. 'The big red truck.' What did it do? Nothing yet. A sentence needs both parts.

words.d: a group of words that tells a whole thought

look.title: Half a Thought
look.text: Look at these two lines. Line one: 'My brother.' Line two: 'My brother ate the last cookie.' Read line one. Wait for more. Nothing comes. Read line two. Now you know the whole story.
look.prompt: What does line two have that line one is missing?

check.q: What does a sentence tell?
check.why: A sentence tells who or what, and what happened. It is a whole thought.

check.q: Which one is a sentence?
check.why: 'The dog ran' tells who (the dog) and what happened (ran). The others are missing a part.

check.q: 'Jumped high.' What is missing?
check.why: 'Jumped high' tells what happened. It does not tell who did it.

lessons.title: A Capital and an End Mark
lessons.mainIdea: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a mark.
reading: Look at this: 'the dog ran' Something is off. It has no start. It has no stop. Now look: 'The dog ran.' The big T says 'Start here.' The dot says 'Stop here.'
A sentence starts with a *capital letter*. That is the big form of a letter. T, not t. It ends with an *end mark*. A period is a dot. It is the most common end mark.
There are three end marks. A period (.) ends a plain sentence. A question mark (?) ends a question. An exclamation point (!) ends a sentence with big feeling. Wow! Every sentence needs one.

words.d: the big form of a letter, like T instead of t
a period, question mark or exclamation point at the end of a sentence

look.title: End Marks in a Short Story
look.cite: counted for this lesson in a short story written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which end mark did the writer use most? Why do you think that is?

check.q: How does a sentence start?
check.why: A sentence starts with a capital letter, the big form of the letter.

check.q: Which end mark ends a plain sentence?
check.why: A period is a dot. It ends a plain sentence that tells something.

check.q: Which sentence is written the right way?
check.why: It starts with a capital T and ends with a period. Both are needed.

lessons.title: Naming Words
lessons.mainIdea: A noun names a person, a place or a thing.
reading: Look around the room. Desk. Window. Teacher. Book. Each word names something you can see. Now think of places. School. Park. Chicago. Those are names too.
A word that names a person, a place or a thing is a *noun*. Girl is a noun. Beach is a noun. Apple is a noun. Every sentence has one. 'The bus stopped.' Bus is the noun.
Find the noun in each sentence. 'My dog barked.' The noun is dog. 'The rain fell.' The noun is rain. Ask yourself: what is this sentence about? That word is the noun.

words.d: a word that names a person, a place or a thing

look.title: Nouns at the Bus Stop
look.text: Picture a bus stop in the morning. A girl holds a backpack. A man reads a paper. A bus pulls up. A dog waits by the bench. Every thing you just pictured has a name.
look.prompt: Name four nouns from the picture. Which ones are people? Which are things?

check.q: What does a noun do?
choices: It names a person, place or thing
check.why: A noun is a naming word. It names people, places and things.

check.q: Which word is a noun?
check.why: 'Apple' names a thing. 'Jump' is an action and 'quickly' is not a name.

check.q: 'The rain fell.' Which word is the noun?
check.why: 'Rain' names the thing the sentence is about. That is the noun.

lessons.title: Action Words
lessons.mainIdea: A verb tells what someone or something does.
reading: Watch a kid at the park. She runs. She jumps. She climbs. She slides. Each word tells what she does. Runs, jumps, climbs, slides. These are action words.
A word that tells what someone or something does is a *verb*. 'The frog hops.' Hops is the verb. 'Dad cooks.' Cooks is the verb. A sentence needs a verb to happen.
Put a noun and a verb together. Now you have a sentence. Birds fly. Babies cry. Bells ring. Two words each. Each one is a whole thought.

words.d: a word that tells what someone or something does

look.title: One Minute at Recess
look.text: Look at the playground for one minute. Sam kicks a ball. Lily swings. Two boys race. A girl reads under a tree. A teacher waves. Every person is doing something.
look.prompt: Name three verbs from the playground. What is the noun that goes with each one?

check.q: What does a verb tell?
check.why: A verb is an action word. It tells what someone or something does.

check.q: 'The frog hops.' Which word is the verb?
check.why: 'Hops' tells what the frog does. That is the verb.

check.q: Which two words make a whole sentence?
check.why: 'Birds' is the noun and 'fly' is the verb. Together they tell a whole thought.

lessons.title: Describing Words
lessons.mainIdea: A describing word tells more about a noun, like its size or color.
reading: Here is a sentence. 'The dog ran.' Now here is a better one. 'The big brown dog ran.' Can you see the dog now? Big tells its size. Brown tells its color.
A word that tells more about a noun is a *describing word*. Big, small, red, soft, loud, wet. It sits in front of the noun. 'A red ball.' 'A soft blanket.' 'A loud truck.'
Describing words help a reader see. 'I ate a cookie' is fine. 'I ate a warm, gooey cookie' is better. Pick words that show what you mean. Do not add too many.

words.d: a word that tells more about a noun, like big, red or soft

look.title: Two Cats
look.text: Look at two cats on a wall. One is a tiny gray kitten with soft fur. One is a huge black cat with a torn ear. If you just said 'a cat,' nobody would know which one you meant.
look.prompt: Which describing words help you tell the two cats apart?

check.q: 'The big brown dog ran.' Which words describe the dog?
check.why: 'Big' tells the size and 'brown' tells the color. They tell more about the dog.

check.q: Where does a describing word usually sit?
check.why: A describing word sits in front of the noun it tells about. 'A red ball.'

check.q: Why use describing words?
check.why: Describing words help the reader picture the thing. A warm, gooey cookie is easy to see.

lessons.title: Telling and Asking
lessons.mainIdea: A telling sentence ends with a period, and an asking sentence ends with a question mark.
reading: Read these two lines. 'You have a dog.' 'Do you have a dog?' The first one tells you something. The second one wants to know. Same words, almost. Different job.
A *telling sentence* gives you news. It ends with a period. 'It is raining.' An *asking sentence* wants an answer. It ends with a question mark. 'Is it raining?'
Asking sentences often start with special words. Who, what, where, when, why, how. Do, is, can, are. If you see one of those at the start, get ready for a question mark.

words.d: a sentence that gives news and ends with a period
a sentence that asks and ends with a question mark

look.title: At the Door
look.text: Listen at the door. 'Can I come in?' 'The door is open.' 'Where are my shoes?' 'They are by the bed.' One person keeps asking. The other person keeps telling.
look.prompt: Which lines need a question mark? How do you know?

check.q: How does an asking sentence end?
check.why: An asking sentence wants an answer. It ends with a question mark.

check.q: Which one is a telling sentence?
check.why: 'The bus is late' gives news. It ends with a period, so it is a telling sentence.

check.q: A sentence starts with 'Where.' What end mark will it need?
check.why: 'Where' starts a question. Questions end with a question mark.

lessons.title: Words in Order
lessons.mainIdea: The words in a sentence have to be in an order that makes sense.
reading: Read this. 'Ate the pizza I.' It is a mess. All the words are real. But the order is wrong. Now fix it. 'I ate the pizza.' Same words. Now it makes sense.
Word *order* is the way the words line up. Most sentences go like this. First, who. Then, what they did. Then, what it was about. 'Mia kicked the ball.' Who, did what, to what.
When a sentence sounds silly, check the order. Say it out loud. Move the words around. 'Park the to went we.' Try again. 'We went to the park.' There it is.

words.d: the way words line up in a sentence

look.title: Word Cards on the Rug
look.text: Four word cards lie on the rug. 'fish' 'The' 'swam' 'away.' Push them into a line. Which word goes first? The one with the capital letter. Then who. Then what it did.
look.prompt: What is the sentence when the cards are in the right order?

check.q: Which order makes sense?
check.why: 'Sam ate the cake' goes who, did what, to what. That order makes sense.

check.q: What usually comes first in a sentence?
check.why: Most sentences start with who or what. Then comes what they did.

check.q: A sentence sounds silly. What should you check?
check.why: If the words are real but it sounds silly, the order is probably wrong.

lessons.title: One Good Sentence
lessons.mainIdea: To write one good sentence, look at a picture, say who and what happened, and leave spaces.
reading: Look at a picture of a girl on a bike. Say what you see. 'The girl rides her bike.' Say it out loud. Count the words. Five. Now write those five words down.
Leave a *space* between each word. 'Thegirlridesherbike' is one long blob. Nobody can read it. 'The girl rides her bike.' Now each word stands alone. Put a finger between the words.
Check your sentence. Does it start with a capital? Does it end with a mark? Does it tell who and what happened? Are there spaces? If yes, you wrote a good sentence.

words.d: the empty gap between two words

look.title: The Picture on the Wall
look.text: Look at a picture. A boy sits in the grass. He holds a red kite. The wind pulls the kite up. His hat is about to blow off. There is a lot to say. Pick one thing.
look.prompt: What one sentence would you write about this picture? Who is it about? What happens?

check.q: What goes between words when you write?
check.why: A space is the empty gap between words. It lets each word stand alone.

check.q: Why is 'Thegirlridesherbike' hard to read?
check.why: With no spaces, the words run together into one blob. Nobody can find the words.

check.q: What should you do first when writing about a picture?
choices: Say out loud what you see
check.why: Say your sentence out loud first. Then count the words and write them down.

review.why: A sentence is a group of words that tells a whole thought: who and what happened.

review.q: Which end mark shows big feeling?
review.why: An exclamation point ends a sentence with big feeling. 'Wow!'

review.q: 'The baby cried.' Which word is the verb?
review.why: 'Cried' tells what the baby did. That is the verb.

review.q: Which word is a describing word?
review.why: 'Soft' tells more about a noun. 'Run' is a verb and 'chair' is a noun.

review.q: Which sentence needs a question mark?
review.why: 'Do you like pizza' asks something. It needs a question mark.

choices: A capital and an end mark
review.why: It has a noun and a verb. It needs a capital T and a period to be a full sentence.
